screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will learn why careful relational design matters in Azure S Q L. A well-designed schema protects data integrity, improves query performance, and makes scaling predictable. We'll connect high-level principles like normalization with practical choices such as data types, clustered and non-clustered indexes, and constraint design. You will see a concrete star schema example for analytics with dimension and fact tables, and T-S Q L snippets that create keys, constraints, and indexes. Practical trade-offs are central: normalization reduces redundancy but can increase join cost; denormalization speeds reads but risks update complexity. We'll cover when to prefer INT over BIGINT, why dates use native date types, and how indexes change read/write performance. By the end you'll understand how to map business requirements to table structures and indexing strategies, and how to test them with representative data. Consider a sales reporting pipeline: the schema you choose directly affects how fast reports run and how hard it is to keep data accurate. Ready to explore best practices, concrete T-S Q L examples, and common mistakes to avoid?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical engineering tasks you will perform in Azure S Q L. First, you'll apply best practices for schema design to support performance and scalability, which means translating business rules into tables, keys, and relationships that reduce unnecessary work for queries. Second, you'll understand how data type choices affect storage and query speed; for example, using an INT when values fit saves space and input and output compared with a larger integer type. Third, you'll implement indexing strategies — clustered and non-clustered — to speed common queries while being mindful of write overhead. Fourth, you'll enforce data integrity with primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints and deploy tables with T-S Q L. Each objective includes hands-on T-S Q L so you leave with both reasoning skills and runnable code. These skills matter because schema and index choices determine how fast reports run, how costly storage becomes, and how safe your data remains under concurrent updates. As you work through examples, test designs with sample data and query patterns to confirm real-world behavior.

screens.title: Why database design matters in Azure SQL
screens.narratorSegment: Database design is not an academic exercise—it's the foundation for performance and reliable systems in Azure S Q L. A clear schema organizes data so queries can find rows quickly and updates remain consistent. For transactional workloads, normalization reduces redundancy and avoids inconsistent updates; for analytical workloads, a measured degree of denormalization reduces expensive joins and speeds reads. Consider two teams: one models orders with highly normalized tables and many joins for reporting, the other uses a denormalized fact table with foreign keys to small dimension tables. The first can suffer slow report queries; the second simplifies reads but increases complexity when updating attributes. In Azure S Q L, these choices also affect storage costs and IO pressure. A practical example: using surrogate integer keys for dimensions keeps indexes compact and joins efficient for large fact tables. A common misconception is that more normalization always equals better design—this ignores query patterns. Before finalizing a design, test with realistic queries and data sizes. Ask: does this schema make the common queries fast, and can we keep integrity without excessive write cost?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Why design matters
Definition & claim

Good schema design organizes columns and tables to reduce redundancy, enforce integrity, and speed queries. In Azure SQL, this reduces I/O and helps the optimizer choose efficient plans.

Key points
  • Normalized schemas reduce redundancy and support safe updates.
  • Denormalization can be used for analytical queries to reduce joins.
  • Surrogate integer keys often improve index compactness on large tables.
  • Always test design choices with representative queries and data.
Key Takeaway

Design to match the workload: integrity-first for OLTP, read-performance-first for analytical stores.

Concrete example
In a sales reporting system, a fact table holds millions of rows. Use surrogate keys (integers) for joins and keep dimensions narrow so joins use small, cache-friendly indexes. Avoid storing dates as text; use date/datetime types so queries and indexes behave predictably.
Common misconception
More normalization is always better.
Normalization helps integrity but can push work into query-time joins. Choose the right balance for your workload.

screens.title: Normalization vs Denormalization
screens.narratorSegment: Normalization is the process of organizing tables and columns to eliminate redundancy and maintain integrity. Normal forms define progressive rules; in transactional systems, applying 1NF through 3NF often prevents update anomalies and makes transactions predictable. Denormalization intentionally introduces redundancy to improve read performance, which is common in data warehouses. For example, a star schema keeps a central fact table with foreign keys to smaller dimension tables. The fact table may be denormalized to include pre-calculated attributes to speed queries. A concrete scenario: a reporting query that joins orders, products, and customers across millions of rows will usually run faster if common attributes are pre-joined in a dimension or materialized view rather than joining many normalized tables at query time. A typical misconception is to apply strict normalization by default; that can produce complex queries and slow reports. Instead, analyze query patterns: if read patterns dominate and joins are expensive, denormalize selectively or use pre-aggregation. Always validate by running representative queries against sample data and measuring improvement before committing to denormalization. Normalization vs Denormalization means use normalization for transactional integrity and denormalization in analytical designs to reduce join cost — validate with query tests.. In practical terms, when to normalize, when to denormalize for analytics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Normalization vs Denormalization
Normalized (OLTP)
  • Reduces redundancy and update anomalies.
  • Good for many small transactions and consistent updates.
  • May require many joins for complex queries.
Mnemonic: Normalize to maintain single source of truth.
Denormalized / Star Schema (OLAP)
  • Redundancy reduces join complexity and speeds reads.
  • Fact table with surrogate keys links to small dimension tables.
  • Requires ETL discipline to keep dimension attributes consistent.
Mnemonic: Denormalize to optimize read-heavy reporting.
Scenario and guidance
If your workload is analytics and reporting over very large row counts, prefer a star schema and selective denormalization. If your workload is high-volume transactional processing with many concurrent writes, prefer normalized designs to ensure correct updates and smaller transactional scope.

screens.title: Choosing Data Types
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right data type matters because it directly affects storage size, input and output, and how the optimizer uses indexes. The guiding rule is: use the smallest type that accurately represents your data. For integers, prefer INT when values will stay under two billion; BIGINT is reserved for very large counters, such as ever-growing fact table identities. For strings, use NVARCHAR when you need Unicode support; NVARCHAR(255) is suitable for product names that rarely exceed that length. Avoid VARCHAR(MAX) or NVARCHAR(MAX) unless you genuinely need very large text because these types can change storage behavior and performance. For dates, use DATE, DATETIME, or DATETIME2; storing dates as strings prevents date arithmetic and indexing efficiency. A concrete example: storing an OrderDate as DATE allows range queries and efficient index seeks; storing it as NVARCHAR forces the engine to convert or perform scans. A common misconception is that larger types are 'safer'—they are, but they increase storage and memory pressure at scale. Always profile storage and input and output with representative rows to see the cumulative effect of type choices. Choosing Data Types means pick the smallest precise type: it reduces storage, improves index density, and speeds query execution.. In practical terms, size, accuracy, and the cost of using the wrong type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Data Types
Type choices and impact
  • INT vs BIGINT: choose INT unless you expect >2B values.
  • NVARCHAR supports Unicode; prefer it when international data is possible.
  • Use DATE/DATETIME/DATETIME2 for date operations and indexing.
  • Avoid MAX types unless truly necessary; they change storage behavior.
Concrete example
If ProductName fits within 255 characters, prefer NVARCHAR(255) instead of NVARCHAR(MAX). If OrderDate stores only the date part, use DATE for smaller storage and faster range scans.
Tip: Small type savings multiply across millions of rows. Test storage footprint after choosing types.

screens.title: Indexes: Clustered and Non-clustered
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes are data structures that speed reads by organizing or pointing to rows, but they also add write and storage overhead. A clustered index defines the physical order of rows in a table and typically maps to the primary key; because a table can have only one clustered index, choose it carefully for columns frequently used in range queries, ORDER BY, or joins. A non-clustered index stores an ordered structure that references row locations; you can create many of these to serve common WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY patterns. Consider a table where OrderDate is frequently filtered: creating a non-clustered index on OrderDate can make these queries seek instead of scan. However, each index must be maintained on insert, update, or delete, so over-indexing slows writes. Selectivity matters: narrow indexes on highly selective columns yield good benefit. A misconception is that adding indexes always improves performance; in write-heavy tables, each index adds cost. Test by measuring query execution plans and write latency before and after adding indexes. Think of indexes as targeted accelerators: use them where query patterns demand faster lookups.

keyIdea.title: Index insight
keyIdea.text: Clustered index orders rows physically; non-clustered indexes provide lookup paths. Balance read benefits against write and storage costs.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Indexes
Clustered Index

Defines physical row order. One per table. Ideal for primary key or range-based queries.

Non-clustered Index

Stores a logical ordering with pointers to rows. Multiple per table. Good for WHERE and JOIN columns.

Design tips
  • Index selective columns with many distinct values.
  • Consider covering indexes to avoid lookups when possible.
  • Monitor write impact: index maintenance affects inserts/updates/deletes.
Common-mistake

Adding many indexes improves reads but can dramatically slow heavy write workloads. Test the balance.

screens.title: Index Design Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A deliberate index design process yields the best balance between read performance and write cost. Start by profiling query patterns: find the most frequent and slowest queries. Next, examine predicate columns: if a column is often used in WHERE clauses and has high selectivity, it is a candidate for a non-clustered index. Then consider covering indexes by including additional columns so queries can be satisfied from the index alone without lookups. For range or ordering queries, evaluate whether the clustered index should be placed on that key. After making changes, test with representative inserts, updates, and deletes to measure write impact. If write performance degrades unacceptably, consolidate indexes or explore filtered indexes for subsets of data. A misconception is that index selectivity is the only factor: column width, fragmentation, and maintenance windows matter too. Example: for a FactSales table, a composite non-clustered index on (DateKey, ProductKey) can accelerate common date-and-product filters, but each insert into FactSales also updates that index. Monitor and iterate: create, test, measure, and revise. This iterative loop is the practical path to an effective index strategy.

keyIdea.title: Design loop
keyIdea.text: Profile queries, choose selective indexes, consider covering and filtered indexes, then test write/read performance and iterate.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Index Design
Index design steps
1.
Profile queries and identify the most frequent predicates and joins.
2.
Choose columns with high selectivity for non-clustered indexes.
3.
Consider included columns to create covering indexes and avoid lookups.
4.
Test with representative write workloads and measure maintenance costs.
Example
For FactSales, a composite index on (DateKey, ProductKey) speeds date-and-product filters. If most queries also select SalesAmount, include it in the index to cover the query and avoid lookups.
Check your understanding: which indexes hurt heavy insert rates most? The ones with many included wide columns and low selectivity.

screens.title: Constraints and Data Integrity
screens.narratorSegment: Constraints are the language the database uses to enforce data integrity. Primary keys guarantee a unique identity for each row and usually back the clustered index. Foreign keys enforce referential integrity, preventing orphaned rows by ensuring a child value exists in the parent table. Unique constraints prevent duplicates on columns or column groups, while check constraints validate domain rules such as non-negative quantities. Default constraints provide a value when none is supplied, which simplifies insert logic. For example, using a CHECK constraint to ensure EffectiveDate is less than or equal to ExpiryDate prevents invalid timelines in a product dimension. A common mistake is relying solely on application logic for integrity; network issues or multiple clients can bypass application checks. Database constraints are the last line of defense and are enforced consistently. When adding foreign keys in very large fact tables, be mindful of cascading deletes and the impact on load operations; sometimes referential checks are enforced at ETL time with controlled loading. Always document constraint rationale so future maintainers understand why rules exist. Constraints and Data Integrity means use database constraints as the authoritative enforcement of data rules; they protect against application or process errors.. In practical terms, primary keys, foreign keys, unique, check, and default constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Constraints
Primary Key
Uniquely identifies rows; often used as clustered index for fast lookups.
Foreign Key
Enforces referential integrity between tables to prevent orphaned rows.
Unique / Check / Default
Unique prevents duplicates; Check enforces domain rules; Default supplies values when none provided.
Practical guidance
Use constraints to make your schema self-validating. In ETL scenarios, plan constraint enforcement and batch operations so loads are efficient while integrity is preserved.

T-SQL (read-only example)
-- Create a Dimension Table for Products
CREATE TABLE DimProduct (
  ProductKey INT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  ProductID NVARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  ProductName NVARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  ProductCategory NVARCHAR(100),
  ProductSubcategory NVARCHAR(100),
  UnitPrice DECIMAL(10, 2) NOT NULL,
  EffectiveDate DATE NOT NULL,
  ExpiryDate DATE NOT NULL,
  IsCurrent BIT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  CONSTRAINT CHK_ProductDates CHECK (EffectiveDate <= ExpiryDate)
);

-- Create a Dimension Table for Dates
CREATE TABLE DimDate (
  DateKey INT PRIMARY KEY, -- YYYYMMDD format
  FullDate DATE NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  DayOfMonth INT NOT NULL,
  Month INT NOT NULL,
  Year INT NOT NULL,
  DayOfWeek NVARCHAR(10),
  IsWeekend BIT NOT NULL
);

-- Create a Fact Table for Sales
CREATE TABLE FactSales (
  SalesKey BIGINT IDENTITY(1,1) PRIMARY KEY,
  DateKey INT NOT NULL,
  ProductKey INT NOT NULL,
  CustomerKey INT NOT NULL,
  OrderQuantity INT NOT NULL,
  SalesAmount DECIMAL(18, 2) NOT NULL,
  DiscountAmount DECIMAL(18, 2) DEFAULT 0.00,
  OrderDate DATETIME DEFAULT GETDATE(),
  CONSTRAINT FK_FactSales_DimDate FOREIGN KEY (DateKey) REFERENCES DimDate(DateKey),
  CONSTRAINT FK_FactSales_DimProduct FOREIGN KEY (ProductKey) REFERENCES DimProduct(ProductKey),
  CONSTRAINT CHK_OrderQuantity CHECK (OrderQuantity > 0),
  CONSTRAINT CHK_SalesAmount CHECK (SalesAmount >= 0)
);

-- Add a non-clustered index for common query patterns
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_FactSales_OrderDate ON FactSales (OrderDate);
Notes
Surrogate keys decouple from source keys. Use CHECK constraints for simple data hygiene. Non-clustered indexes accelerate date-based filters but add write cost.

screens.title: Indexing Examples and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes can accelerate queries or, when misapplied, become a liability. A well-chosen index on a selective column can convert a scan into a seek, lowering input and output and latency. Conversely, an index on a low-selectivity column—such as a flag used in many rows—rarely helps and can actually slow queries because the optimizer still needs to fetch many rows. Another pitfall is creating wide indexes that include many large columns; these increase storage and memory pressure on the engine. Over time, fragmentation also reduces index efficiency and requires maintenance like rebuilding or reorganizing. Consider an index created on ProductName (NVARCHAR(255)): if ProductName repeats often, the index provides little benefit. A better strategy is to put a non-clustered index on ProductID or ProductKey, which are compact and selective. For write-heavy fact tables, prefer narrower indexes and consider filtered indexes for hot partitions. The practical rule is to measure: add an index, run representative queries and writes, and compare plans and timing. Iteration and monitoring are critical. Good index

screens.title: Testing and Validating Schema Choices
screens.narratorSegment: Testing is the final and essential step in schema design. Begin by generating representative data volumes and distribution—synthetic data that matches cardinalities, skew, and growth patterns. Run the most common and the most expensive queries while capturing execution plans and timing. Compare plans before and after schema or index changes. Watch for changes in logical reads and whether seeks replace scans. Also measure write performance: inserts, updates, and deletes must stay within acceptable latency windows. If adding indexes helps reads but slows writes too much, consider filtered or covering indexes, or schedule maintenance windows for rebuilds. Another dimension is concurrency: simulate multiple clients to see lock contention or blocking. A common mistake is validating only with tiny samples; the optimizer and statistics behave differently at scale. Document your tests, data shapes, and results so stakeholders understand why a design was chosen. The goal is not perfection but an evidence-based balance that meets both query latency and data integrity requirements. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you will learn why careful relational design matters in Azure S Q L. A well-designed schema protects data integrity, improves query performance, and makes scaling predictable. We'll connect high-level principles like normalization with practical choices such as data types, clustered and non-clustered indexes, and constraint design. You will see a concrete star schema example for analytics with dimension and fact tables, and T-S Q L snippets that create keys, constraints, and indexes. Practical trade-offs are central: normalization reduces redundancy but can increase join cost; denormalization speeds reads but risks update complexity. We'll cover when to prefer INT over BIGINT, why dates use native date types, and how indexes change read/write performance. By the end you'll understand how to map business requirements to table structures and indexing strategies, and how to test them with representative data. Consider a sales reporting pipeline: the schema you choose directly affects how fast reports run and how hard it is to keep data accurate. Ready to explore best practices, concrete T-S Q L examples, and common mistakes to avoid?

These objectives map to practical engineering tasks you will perform in Azure S Q L. First, you'll apply best practices for schema design to support performance and scalability, which means translating business rules into tables, keys, and relationships that reduce unnecessary work for queries. Second, you'll understand how data type choices affect storage and query speed; for example, using an INT when values fit saves space and input and output compared with a larger integer type. Third, you'll implement indexing strategies — clustered and non-clustered — to speed common queries while being mindful of write overhead. Fourth, you'll enforce data integrity with primary keys, foreign keys, and constraints and deploy tables with T-S Q L. Each objective includes hands-on T-S Q L so you leave with both reasoning skills and runnable code. These skills matter because schema and index choices determine how fast reports run, how costly storage becomes, and how safe your data remains under concurrent updates. As you work through examples, test designs with sample data and query patterns to confirm real-world behavior.

This second objectives slide narrows toward practical tests and common pitfalls. You will implement a simple star schema—fact and dimension tables—then insert sample rows and run SELECT queries to verify behavior. You will add non-clustered indexes on frequently filtered columns and observe query speed. You will write constraints: primary keys to prevent duplicates, foreign keys to avoid orphaned rows, check constraints to validate domain rules, and default constraints to simplify inserts. Importantly, you will learn to test with representative data and query patterns; tests reveal whether your indexing choice improves real queries or just looks good in theory. A frequent mistake is over-indexing: many indexes slow down writes and maintenance. Another common error is using wide data types that increase storage and input and output; small choices like INT vs BIGINT accumulate at scale. By practicing with the provided T-S Q L and sample inserts you will build intuition about trade-offs and be able to justify design decisions to stakeholders.

Database design is not an academic exercise—it's the foundation for performance and reliable systems in Azure S Q L. A clear schema organizes data so queries can find rows quickly and updates remain consistent. For transactional workloads, normalization reduces redundancy and avoids inconsistent updates; for analytical workloads, a measured degree of denormalization reduces expensive joins and speeds reads. Consider two teams: one models orders with highly normalized tables and many joins for reporting, the other uses a denormalized fact table with foreign keys to small dimension tables. The first can suffer slow report queries; the second simplifies reads but increases complexity when updating attributes. In Azure S Q L, these choices also affect storage costs and IO pressure. A practical example: using surrogate integer keys for dimensions keeps indexes compact and joins efficient for large fact tables. A common misconception is that more normalization always equals better design—this ignores query patterns. Before finalizing a design, test with realistic queries and data sizes. Ask: does this schema make the common queries fast, and can we keep integrity without excessive write cost?

Normalization is the process of organizing tables and columns to eliminate redundancy and maintain integrity. Normal forms define progressive rules; in transactional systems, applying 1NF through 3NF often prevents update anomalies and makes transactions predictable. Denormalization intentionally introduces redundancy to improve read performance, which is common in data warehouses. For example, a star schema keeps a central fact table with foreign keys to smaller dimension tables. The fact table may be denormalized to include pre-calculated attributes to speed queries. A concrete scenario: a reporting query that joins orders, products, and customers across millions of rows will usually run faster if common attributes are pre-joined in a dimension or materialized view rather than joining many normalized tables at query time. A typical misconception is to apply strict normalization by default; that can produce complex queries and slow reports. Instead, analyze query patterns: if read patterns dominate and joins are expensive, denormalize selectively or use pre-aggregation. Always validate by running representative queries against sample data and measuring improvement before committing to denormalization. Normalization vs Denormalization means use normalization for transactional integrity and denormalization in analytical designs to reduce join cost — validate with query tests.. In practical terms, when to normalize, when to denormalize for analytics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right data type matters because it directly affects storage size, input and output, and how the optimizer uses indexes. The guiding rule is: use the smallest type that accurately represents your data. For integers, prefer INT when values will stay under two billion; BIGINT is reserved for very large counters, such as ever-growing fact table identities. For strings, use NVARCHAR when you need Unicode support; NVARCHAR(255) is suitable for product names that rarely exceed that length. Avoid VARCHAR(MAX) or NVARCHAR(MAX) unless you genuinely need very large text because these types can change storage behavior and performance. For dates, use DATE, DATETIME, or DATETIME2; storing dates as strings prevents date arithmetic and indexing efficiency. A concrete example: storing an OrderDate as DATE allows range queries and efficient index seeks; storing it as NVARCHAR forces the engine to convert or perform scans. A common misconception is that larger types are 'safer'—they are, but they increase storage and memory pressure at scale. Always profile storage and input and output with representative rows to see the cumulative effect of type choices. Choosing Data Types means pick the smallest precise type: it reduces storage, improves index density, and speeds query execution.. In practical terms, size, accuracy, and the cost of using the wrong type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Indexes are data structures that speed reads by organizing or pointing to rows, but they also add write and storage overhead. A clustered index defines the physical order of rows in a table and typically maps to the primary key; because a table can have only one clustered index, choose it carefully for columns frequently used in range queries, ORDER BY, or joins. A non-clustered index stores an ordered structure that references row locations; you can create many of these to serve common WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY patterns. Consider a table where OrderDate is frequently filtered: creating a non-clustered index on OrderDate can make these queries seek instead of scan. However, each index must be maintained on insert, update, or delete, so over-indexing slows writes. Selectivity matters: narrow indexes on highly selective columns yield good benefit. A misconception is that adding indexes always improves performance; in write-heavy tables, each index adds cost. Test by measuring query execution plans and write latency before and after adding indexes. Think of indexes as targeted accelerators: use them where query patterns demand faster lookups.

A deliberate index design process yields the best balance between read performance and write cost. Start by profiling query patterns: find the most frequent and slowest queries. Next, examine predicate columns: if a column is often used in WHERE clauses and has high selectivity, it is a candidate for a non-clustered index. Then consider covering indexes by including additional columns so queries can be satisfied from the index alone without lookups. For range or ordering queries, evaluate whether the clustered index should be placed on that key. After making changes, test with representative inserts, updates, and deletes to measure write impact. If write performance degrades unacceptably, consolidate indexes or explore filtered indexes for subsets of data. A misconception is that index selectivity is the only factor: column width, fragmentation, and maintenance windows matter too. Example: for a FactSales table, a composite non-clustered index on (DateKey, ProductKey) can accelerate common date-and-product filters, but each insert into FactSales also updates that index. Monitor and iterate: create, test, measure, and revise. This iterative loop is the practical path to an effective index strategy.

Constraints are the language the database uses to enforce data integrity. Primary keys guarantee a unique identity for each row and usually back the clustered index. Foreign keys enforce referential integrity, preventing orphaned rows by ensuring a child value exists in the parent table. Unique constraints prevent duplicates on columns or column groups, while check constraints validate domain rules such as non-negative quantities. Default constraints provide a value when none is supplied, which simplifies insert logic. For example, using a CHECK constraint to ensure EffectiveDate is less than or equal to ExpiryDate prevents invalid timelines in a product dimension. A common mistake is relying solely on application logic for integrity; network issues or multiple clients can bypass application checks. Database constraints are the last line of defense and are enforced consistently. When adding foreign keys in very large fact tables, be mindful of cascading deletes and the impact on load operations; sometimes referential checks are enforced at ETL time with controlled loading. Always document constraint rationale so future maintainers understand why rules exist. Constraints and Data Integrity means use database constraints as the authoritative enforcement of data rules; they protect against application or process errors.. In practical terms, primary keys, foreign keys, unique, check, and default constraints. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dimension tables often use surrogate integer keys with IDENTITY to decouple from source system business keys. The DimProduct table uses a primary key ProductKey and a business key ProductID marked unique. DimDate uses DateKey in YYYYMMDD format, which simplifies joins. The FactSales table has a BIGINT identity primary key and foreign keys to the dimension tables. Note the use of appropriate types: DECIMAL for monetary amounts, INT for keys, and DATETIME for timestamps. The script also includes CHECK constraints for data quality, like ensuring OrderQuantity is greater than zero. Indexes can accelerate queries or, when misapplied, become a liability. A well-chosen index on a selective column can convert a scan into a seek, lowering input and output and latency. Conversely, an index on a low-selectivity column—such as a flag used in many rows—rarely helps and can actually slow queries because the optimizer still needs to fetch many rows. Another pitfall is creating wide indexes that include many large columns; these increase storage and memory pressure on the engine. Over time, fragmentation also reduces index efficiency and requires maintenance like rebuilding or reorganizing. Consider an index created on ProductName (NVARCHAR(255)): if ProductName repeats often, the index provides little benefit. A better strategy is to put a non-clustered index on ProductID or ProductKey, which are compact and selective. For write-heavy fact tables, prefer narrower indexes and consider filtered indexes for hot partitions. The practical rule is to measure: add an index, run representative queries and writes, and compare plans and timing. Iteration and monitoring are critical. Testing is the final and essential step in schema design. Begin by generating representative data volumes and distribution—synthetic data that matches cardinalities, skew, and growth patterns. Run the most common and the most expensive queries while capturing execution plans and timing. Compare plans before and after schema or index changes. Watch for changes in logical reads and whether seeks replace scans. Also measure write performance: inserts, updates, and deletes must stay within acceptable latency windows. If adding indexes helps reads but slows writes too much, consider filtered or covering indexes, or schedule maintenance windows for rebuilds. Another dimension is concurrency: simulate multiple clients to see lock contention or blocking. A common mistake is validating only with tiny samples; the optimizer and statistics behave differently at scale. Document your tests, data shapes, and results so stakeholders understand why a design was chosen. The goal is not perfection but an evidence-based balance that meets both query latency and data integrity requirements. Let's summarize the key concepts you should carry forward. Normalization reduces redundancy and supports transactional integrity; denormalization can speed analytical queries by reducing joins. Data types influence storage and performance—choose the smallest precise type and use native date types for date arithmetic. Clustered indexes define physical storage order and are typically chosen for primary keys or range queries. Non-clustered indexes provide lookup paths for WHERE and JOIN predicates but add write overhead. These core ideas form the basis of schema design decisions in Azure S Q L.
